ky_emerald_city.blurb:
Emerald City is a sandstone wall in the Natural Bridge area of the Red River Gorge, tucked in beside the Lady Slipper cliffs. Most of what is filed here is bouldering, a cluster of problems mostly V0 to V3 beneath the wall, with roped lines from 5.5 to 5.12 above them: a mix of sport, trad and the odd top-rope.

The sandstone is the gorge's typical featured, hold-rich rock, and the harder roped lines are steep enough to feel athletic. Several climbs have a high first bolt, so a stick-clip is handy. A short approach and a sunny face make it a good fit for climbers who want a quick walk and a spread of grades.
ky_emerald_city.approach: A short uphill walk of five to ten minutes on the trail leads to the base of the wall.

wv_south_peak_west_face_main_area.blurb:
The main area of South Peak's west face is the heart of Seneca Rocks, a thin quartzite fin rising above the North Fork valley. Dozens of multi-pitch routes line the face, from beginner-friendly 5.2 lines up to the 5.12s and beyond, with the bulk between 5.7 and 5.10; nearly all are traditional, with a little aid and a few bolted sections.

The classic easy ways to the summit, such as Old Man's Route, are among the most popular climbs in the region, so the lower-grade lines can be crowded on fair weekends. Exposure, pitches that wander between ledges and a summit left by rappel make it a good objective for climbers building trad and multi-pitch skills.
wv_south_peak_west_face_main_area.approach: Cross the footbridge from the parking lot and turn right toward the gap, then cross the creek on boulders and climb the steep switchback trail known as the Stairmaster to the base of the west face. Walk north along the face to the start of your route.

wv_whippoorwill.blurb:
Whippoorwill is a sandstone crag on the shore of Summersville Lake with nearly ninety lines, most of them bolted, about twenty trad routes and a couple of boulders. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.13 with the bulk at 5.10 to 5.12, on big, positive holds with a sunny exposure that makes it a pleasant place to spend a cold day.

Its base sits close to lake level, so the walls are reachable mainly in the drawn-down months of fall and winter; in summer the lower walls are underwater. Climbers who like steep jug-hauling on sandstone and a short walk will find a lot to do.
wv_whippoorwill.approach: From the parking beside Whippoorwill Road, drop down a steep and sometimes muddy trail toward the lake to reach the main area just past the road.

wv_reeds_creek.blurb:
Reeds Creek is a compact limestone sport crag in Pendleton County, between Franklin and Petersburg, with cliffs around sixty feet high. Nearly ninety routes run from 5.6 to 5.12, the bulk between 5.8 and 5.10, on arêtes and dihedrals.

Most climbs need six to ten quickdraws, and a few want some trad gear. The faces catch sun all day, which makes it a favoured winter outing, and the crag is busy enough that the parking can fill up.

nc_laurel_knob.blurb:
Laurel Knob is a big granite dome in the Panthertown area near Cashiers, with a tall face that holds long, committing trad and aid routes, from 5.7 to 5.13 with most at 5.10 and 5.11, and a lone bolted line. Climbs such as Groover, Seconds and Fathom give a taste of the character: sustained, slabby friction and runout sections that reward steady nerves.

It is a serious day out. The hike in is long, so parties start early and plan for a full day. It suits experienced multi-pitch trad climbers comfortable with run-out slab.
nc_laurel_knob.approach: A long, fairly strenuous hike leads in from the end of the gravel access road toward Panthertown: about two hours in and longer out.

az_pond_the.blurb:
The Pond is one of the busiest sport walls in Queen Creek Canyon, a short drive east of Phoenix on the Superior side of the tunnel. The sunny, south-facing tuff is covered in pockets, and the routes run from 5.5 to 5.13 with most at 5.10 and 5.11, plus a few trad lines.

It is a strong pick for newer leaders and mixed-ability groups because there are plenty of moderates on pocketed, positive rock. Expect company on weekends and a warm wall for most of the day.
az_pond_the.approach: Follow the canyon road uphill from the pull-off for roughly three hundred yards to a bridge and pass beneath it. Then scramble over boulders and the creek bed and climb a steep third- and fourth-class section protected by a webbing handline and a rebar ladder to reach the walls.

nl_main_face.blurb:
The Main Face is the largest and most route-rich wall at Flatrock, a pebbly sea cliff a short drive north of St. John's. The rock is solid, mostly vertical conglomerate with the odd roof, and the climbing mixes bolted lines, near-sport routes and trad lines where bolts are sparse, from 5.6 to the 5.13s with most at 5.10 and 5.11.

The best trad climbs sit around 5.9 and 5.10. The cobbled texture makes cams and nuts fiddly, so conservative gear choices are wise on a first visit. It faces east, so it is a morning-sun wall, and summer brings long light, few bugs and whales offshore.
nl_main_face.approach: Walk from the trailhead along the coast path, then follow the cliff top to a shelf at the base of the face; well under fifteen minutes.

ca_a_swan_slab.blurb:
Swan Slab is a roadside granite slab on the north side of Yosemite Valley, directly across from Yosemite Lodge and beneath Yosemite Falls. A short walk gets you to the base, which makes it popular for learning slab technique and for quick top-rope laps; about half of what is filed here is bouldering at its foot.

The routes are mostly low-angle friction and thin-crack climbing on polished granite, from 5.1 to 5.11 with most between 5.6 and 5.9, and the boulder problems run V0 to V8. It suits beginners, guided groups and anyone after a short outing, though the Valley floor gets hot in midsummer.
ca_a_swan_slab.approach: Walk from the parking along the wide dirt path toward the base of the slab, five to ten minutes.

mi_slugg_s_bluff_bouldering.blurb:
Slugg's Bluff is a quartzite crag at Palmer in the Upper Peninsula, about twenty minutes from Marquette, owned by the local climbers' coalition. The boulder problems sit below the main cliff, which also holds sport and traditional routes; most are V0 to V3, with harder lines up to V12.

The quartzite is hard and sharp-edged, so expect crimpy, technical movement on a smaller scale than the cliff above. A local feel prevails and crowds are light, making it a quiet stop for visitors working the Marquette area.
